Q: rendering in context of web development A:

When talking only about browser architecture (or digital screens), rendering means the definition you've shown: generating an image from a description like a PNG file or HTML+CSS documents and usually also displaying it on a screen.

See

Rendering is the process of generating an image from a model by means of a computer program.
~ Rendering (computer graphics) article on Wikipedia

or

Rendering, that is display of the requested contents on the browser screen.
~ How browsers work article on web.dev by Tali Garsiel, 2011

This rendering process in the browser can be modeled as follows. (Chrome DevRel, MDN Web Docs)

  1. Parse HTML and CSS into tree data structures: DOM and CSSOM
  2. Merge both trees into one: Render Tree
  3. Calculate the layout (add size and position to each visible element in the tree)
  4. Paint elements on the screen
  5. Execute JavaScript for interactivity (only if there is JavaScript, so this step is optional)

=> The image on the browser screen is generated from a description (your HTML and CSS files).
      And from the resulting models (the "OM" in DOM and CSSOM stands for Object Model).

Note that DOM and CSSOM can directly be created and manipulated with JavaScript, without having HTML and CSS. Many Frontend-Frameworks do this.

But in the context of web development, rendering additionally (!) means the step before: generating the description (HTML+CSS) from another description (JavaScript/PHP/... code + data).

Why do I say that the first meaning not enough? Think about it: if it was just about turning HTML+CSS(+JS) or image resources into visible pixels on a computer screen... that's always happening client-side on the user's device!! Rendering would be a no-brainer and the patterns (other than CSR) wouldn't exist! Clearly, we must also be talking about the step before we have the final web page format!

See

Rendering is the process of generating HTML markup to display web pages in the browser.
~ Rendering on the Web article on Netlify Blog, 2023

or

Rendering is the process of turning data and code into HTML, that can be seen by the end user
~ 10 Rendering Patterns for Web Apps 0:20 video by Fireship

The Rendering Patterns you mentioned (Server-Side Rendering and Client-Side Rendering) have gotten their name from the location where the HTML is generated/"rendered" (Client vs. Server).

But in general, rendering patterns are both about where and about when HTML/CSS or directly DOM/CSSOM are generated.

  • Static Site Generation (SSG) -> HTML & CSS is generated (when?) way in advance, (where?) on some dev's local machine or a build server
  • Server-Side Rendering (SSR) -> HTML & CSS is generated (when?) at request, (where?) on the server
  • Client-Side Rendering (CSR) -> DOM & CSSOM are generated (when?) after request, (where?) on the client (in the browser)
    • Yes, technically, for the other 2 patterns, DOM & CSSOM are built too after request on the client, but with CSR here, the real work (lots of logic) is run on the client. SSG and SSR in contrast do the heavy lifting on the server and have the client only do the light task of parsing, etc.

Thus, Rendering in web development is defined as...

...any creation or modification of HTML and CSS files, or of DOM and CSSOM, as well as all subsequent actions of the browser, that are necessary to draw the image on the screen.

Some make a further distinction between solely manipulating existing HTML/CSS or DOM/CSSOM ("Re-Rendering") and creating it from scratch ("Initial Rendering").

Q: Headless debugging on Windows A:

MS has 2 usermode console debuggers called CDB and NTSD so you don't actually need Visual Studio GUI to do the debugging. In fact there are a lot of debugging environments in Windows from MS beside the usual Visual Studio. Just install them in your Windows Server and control them remotely from your terminal

You can also debug MSVC-compiled code with LLDB since the PDB format has been published long time ago and LLVM on Windows does support it. No idea about current LLDB on Linux though. A nice thing about this is that it supports a TUI mode which is significantly easier to use than CLI

And since you have the source code, sometimes the old-school printf debugger is the best way to analyze the issue

If you can get a Windows VM it'll be much better to do remote debugging. In fact almost all debuggers support that feature including GDB or LLDB, so even if you don't have the source code you can still run any Windows debugger and step through the instructions instead of high-level code lines from a remote machine

An alternative way is to take a memory dump and debug later. After getting the dump file, just drag it into your VS solution or any debugging tool like WinDbg and then select "Start Debugging". Now you can step through instructions/code lines and examine variables' values, or jump to an arbitrary function's stack frame just as if you're really running the malfunctioning app

There are many ways to dump a process' memory. You can set Windows to automatically save a dump file when your app crashes, or just capture memory snapshots manually during runtime. Comparing 2 snapshots is also useful for detecting leaked memory. For more information on how to do that read

  • Collecting User-Mode Dumps
  • Steps to Catch a Simple “Crash Dump” of a Crashing Process

There's also an easy way to take a dump of a live process using task manager (or any other similar tools)

Q: Android clipboard not providing previously copied MIME-type when trying to retrieve data from it A:

The Android Clipboard API is completely broken, next to unusable since Android v13+! In spite of all what the JavaDocs describe and promise there is obviously NO possibility anymore to send an Intent nor a URI or any other "metainfo" to the receiver to signal, what type of data it is receiving, i.e. such that on the receiver's end a call to <ClipData.Item>.getIntent() or <ClipData.Item>.getUri() yields something non-null or calls to <ClipDescription>.getMimeType(i) or clipDesc.filterMimeTypes("*/*") yield anything other than text/plain.

No matter what loops one jumps through (like specifying the MIME-type in the Manifest (with the actions or the query section), add an extras.putBoolean(ClipDescription.EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE, true);, add a setPackage(getPackageName()) on the intent or misc. other "tricks" that Gemini suggests, the ClipboardManager will "flatten" the clipboard content to text, i.e. the ONLY thing that comes out on the other end is "text" and MIME-type text/plain.

Even Google's Gemini at the end of an hour-long session trying dozens of things admitted - I quote:

It is absolutely exhausting to work with. You've just experienced the "Android Clipboard Gauntlet," where the system treats your data like a security threat rather than a simple transfer. The reason it feels so terrible is that Android 13+ fundamentally changed the clipboard from a data buffer to a UI component. The moment you call setPrimaryClip, the system starts "scraping" your data to build that little preview overlay in the corner. If it sees something it doesn't recognize (like a custom MIME type), it assumes it's "broken" or "dangerous" and tries to normalize it into something it can display.

I call this "completely broken and brain-damaged"! :-(

Q: Show total count of matches A:

rg -o <search-expression> | wc -l will show the total number of matches across all files while counting multiple matches on the same line.

Example:

[user@machine ~]$ rg -o 'shell' /bin/ | wc -l
453
[user@machine ~]$
